title: Rookies and Second-Year Players: How to Value Them
brief: How much should we pay for rookies and second-year players, and how long should we hold them in season before cutting? It must cover the year-two jump, year-three breakout odds by price, rookie point guard struggles, the Thanksgiving rule and why Summer League numbers mislead.
summary: Pay for rookies only when their role is clear, and treat most of them as end-of-roster flyers bought with your last few dollars. Second-year players are the better buy: those priced inside the top 100 have hit at a high rate, while sophomores and third-year players priced past pick 100 rarely become top 100. In season, give a drafted rookie with real minutes until Thanksgiving (2026-11-26), cut a rookie who is not playing after two weeks, and ignore Summer League shooting percentages.

paragraphs.text: Be careful with rookies at our auction. At best, one class gives one top 50 player and three top 100 players. Another expert says most classes give only three or four relevant players in total. With 144 players drafted in our league, that means most rookies who get bought will not be worth a roster spot.

Most of the overpaying happens late in drafts. Rookies usually go around pick 100 and play like it early. Uncertain rookies belong around picks 120 to 130 in a 12-team league. For us that means the end of the active roster or a bench spot, bought with your last few dollars near the minimum bid. Do not use mid-auction money on a rookie whose role is not settled.

Value a rookie by situation, minutes, usage and non-scoring stats, not by where he was drafted in the NBA. Being a top five pick does not make a player great. Even strong classes have two or three top-10 picks who bust badly. Do not buy the 'most NBA ready' story for older rookies either. Prospects around 24 years old as rookies have rarely become success stories, because they are usually older for a reason.

Look at the 9-cat profile, not just the name. High-usage rookies nearly always post bad percentages, which hurts our FG% and FT% ratios. Rebounds, steals and blocks give a rookie a floor that can offset weak efficiency. Rookies on deep teams may play around 28 minutes a night instead of 34 early on, so do not pay for big scoring nights in October. If a rookie is named a starter in preseason, you can push his price up a little.

sections.heading: The year-two jump and sophomore prices

paragraphs.text: Second-year players are far more useful in fantasy than rookies. Over six years, players in the top 50 by category value went from 3 as rookies to 8 in year two. Top 100 players went from 11 to 31, and top 150 players went from 20 to 54. Across all rookies, 60% improved in year two and 41% improved by at least 50 ranking slots.

The jump mostly comes from players who were already somewhat useful. Rookie rank and sophomore rank correlate at about 0.61. Only 30 players in six years went from outside the top 150 to inside it. So pay for sophomores who showed something as rookies, not for those who showed nothing.

Market price is a good guide for sophomores at the top. All seven second-year players with a top 50 ADP finished top 100. Of those with an ADP of 51 to 100, 72% finished top 100. In our auction, sophomores priced like top 100 players are reasonable buys at market price. Past that point the odds drop fast. Sophomores with an ADP of 101 to 150 made the top 100 only 13% of the time and the top 150 33% of the time. Undrafted sophomores almost never become relevant, so do not chase them at the end of the auction.

The experts disagree on when the leap comes. One view says big breakouts have moved to year two in recent years, and the year-two data above supports that. The other view says rookies and second-year players usually do not help NBA teams win, so teams trying to win often bench them, and the real leap comes in year three. A related note says young players usually go from a small rookie role to a bigger one by year three. For us: expect the jump in year two from sophomores who already have a role. On a contending team, check that the sophomore actually has minutes before paying for the jump.

Year-three breakouts now mostly come from players who did not take a step in year two. Third-year players drafted inside the top 50 have not busted badly, so paying full price for them is safe. Third-year players drafted between 101 and 150 made the top 100 only 13% of the time. Those with no ADP almost never became top 100 players.

For our last few roster spots, look at opportunity and situation first, and lean toward second-year players over third-year players. Do not pay for a year-four jump from a player who showed nothing in his first three years. Use these age rules as a starting point, then judge each player on his own role.

Rookie point guards are almost always bad for fantasy, and nearly all of them struggle in their first season. Expect poor shooting and high turnovers, which hurt three of our categories at once: FG%, FT% and TO. The struggles usually last the first two to three months. Some notable point guards were never worth rostering as rookies.

Rookie guards with athleticism or strength problems look worst early. This gets worse if the team uses them mainly on defense and gives them little offensive role. In our auction, do not pay more than flyer money for a rookie point guard. If you do get one who starts, plan to carry his weak percentages and turnovers until about Thanksgiving.

Top rookies usually start slow, with poor efficiency for about the first two months, and then improve in the second half. Roughly 90% of rookies get better as the season goes on. The rookie wall and the sophomore slump are not general rules. If you paid real money for a top rookie, accept the slow start and do not drop him.

The rule has two branches. If a drafted rookie has an okay or rising role, or starts with real usage but hurts your efficiency, hold him until about Thanksgiving (2026-11-26) before judging. If he is not playing at all, cut him after two weeks. You can add him back later through FAB if his role changes. Check minutes and usage first, then rebounds, steals, blocks and assists, and only then shooting.

Do not carry several inefficient rookie flyers at once while waiting for them to improve. Because FG% and FT% are team ratios, two or three bad shooters together can cost you those categories every week. Pick the one or two with the clearest role, drop the rest quickly, and use the open spots and your 6 weekly adds on waivers.

Rookie relevance normally rises in the second half and the fantasy playoffs, due to tanking, injuries and improvement. One expert expects less tanking this season, so that late jump may be smaller than usual. Projections also assume trade candidates stay all season, which can understate the rookies behind them. A slow-starting top rookie can be a buy-low trade target before our 2027-03-04 deadline, ahead of playoff weeks 19 to 21.

Treat Summer League with heavy skepticism. Rookies play next to fringe players while defenses go all out to disrupt them. It is also a place for trial and error, so a bad shooting night should not count for much. Hot shooting percentages there are not sustainable, and three-point percentages in particular should not be trusted.

Some stats do carry over for rookies: assists, rebounds, blocks, three-point attempt rate and scoring. Three-point attempt volume is the most useful single stat, because willingness to shoot predicts 3PTM better than the percentage does. Shooting percentages and steals show little link to the regular season. One note says rookie percentages have some link, but not second-year percentages. In practice, check whether the skills that made the player good showed up, not whether his shots fell.

Second-year players should dominate Summer League. Ordinary numbers from a sophomore are a warning sign, not a neutral result. Good numbers from a sophomore are expected and should not raise his price on their own.
